newsitem.title: USA: MSRB launches exam of muni finance process - aide.
newsitem.headline: MSRB launches exam of muni finance process - aide.

text.p: The MSRB is embarking on a major examination of muni finance to determine if it or other regulators need to adopt rules, set policies or take other steps aimed at curbing conflicts of interest among market players, a top group official said on Friday.

The announcement by Christopher Taylor, executive director of Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, comes amid mounting federal enforcement actions against top financial advisers in the municipal market, including former Lazard Freres & Co. executive Mark Ferber.

Taylor said MSRB staff has been instructed by the 15-member board, which met in Washington Thursday, to "prepare a memorandum with a range of options" in time for the board's February quarterly meeting in Hawaii.
"The board is looking at the totality of the financing," starting with when the issuer first seeks out underwriters, financial advisers and other professionals, Taylor said.

"We want to look real hard at that process and see if there's anything we should be doing to make sure that it is as clean as possible and is in the best interest of the issuer," Taylor said in a telephone press briefing.
Taylor and board Chairman Roger Hayes, managing director of municipal finance for NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, said the panel will examine a range of options.

Hayes said, "You could think about additional disclosures, such as simply shedding more light on who's paying who what and what their relationships are and (whether that will) withstand the scrutiny of the press and issuers?"

In the case of Ferber, a federal jury in August convicted the former adviser to top issuers on 58 out of 61 counts of fraud and corruption involving a $1 million retainer and swap fee-splitting arrangement with Merrill Lynch & Co.
Taylor said regulation writing is not the board's only option. "We'll do whatever we can within our authority," he said.

He noted in 1988 the board uncovered regulatory problems with paying agents, a sector over which the board has not clear authority. Instead of trying to write a rule, the board wrote a letter to the American Bankers Association and "brokered" a meeting with the SEC and issuer groups.
Hayes said, "Everybody on the board reads the paper and hears what's going on. They bring that to the board. These are very serious people that want to do what's right for this industry," he said.
